terms.meaning: The Earth spinning on its own axis, once in about 24 hours.
The Earth going around the Sun, once in nearly 1 year.
The imaginary line through the North and South Poles on which the Earth spins.
The Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, and its shadow falls on the Earth.
The Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, and its shadow falls on the Moon.
The star that seems to stay still, because the Earth’s axis points almost at it.

items.name: Direction of rotation
items.formula: West to East, so anti-clockwise as seen from above the North Pole.

items.name: Day and night
items.formula: The half facing the Sun has day and the other half has night.
items.example: When it is day in India, it is night in the USA.

items.name: Motion of the Sun and stars
items.formula: They only seem to move from East to West, because the Earth turns.
items.example: It is like trees seeming to move past a merry-go-round.

items.name: Foucault pendulum
items.formula: A long heavy pendulum that first showed the Earth’s rotation directly.
items.example: One hangs in the new Parliament building in New Delhi.

items.name: Aryabhata’s boat
items.formula: A person in a moving boat sees the shore move back. In the same way, the stars seem to move west.
items.example: He wrote this in the Aryabhatiya.

items.name: Time for one revolution
items.example: Four such years make about one extra day: 4 × 6 = 24 hours.

items.name: Why seasons happen
items.formula: The tilt of the Earth’s axis, and the Earth’s round shape.
items.example: The tilt stays in the same direction all through the orbit.

items.name: June in India
items.formula: Tilted towards the Sun: rays are more direct, days are longer, and it is summer.
items.example: The longest day in the north is around 21 June.

items.name: December in India
items.formula: Tilted away from the Sun: rays spread out, days are shorter, and it is winter.
items.example: The shortest day in the north is around 22 December.

items.name: Seasons in the two halves
items.formula: They are opposite in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
items.example: December is winter in India and summer in Australia.

items.name: Equal day and night
items.formula: Around 21 March and 23 September, day and night are about 12 hours each everywhere.
items.example: Neither pole is tilted towards the Sun.

items.name: Why the Moon can cover the Sun
items.formula: The Moon is much smaller but much closer, so they look about the same size.
items.example: Your thumb can hide a far-off tree.

items.name: Order in a line
items.formula: Solar: Sun, Moon, Earth. Lunar: Sun, Earth, Moon.
items.example: The body in the middle casts the shadow.

items.name: Watching a solar eclipse
items.formula: Never look with bare eyes, sunglasses or binoculars. Use eclipse goggles or project the image.
items.example: A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes.

items.name: Total lunar eclipse
items.formula: The whole Moon enters the Earth’s shadow and looks dark red.
items.example: It can be seen from a large part of the Earth.

items.name: Transit of Venus
items.formula: Venus crosses the Sun as a tiny black dot.
items.example: It is much bigger than the Moon but so far away that it can never block the Sun.

mistakes.text: Seasons do not happen because the Earth gets closer to the Sun. The Earth is in fact closest in January, which is winter in India.
The Sun does not really rise and set. The Earth’s rotation makes it look that way.
Rotation gives day and night. Revolution with the tilt gives the seasons.
In a solar eclipse the Moon’s shadow falls on Earth. In a lunar eclipse the Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.
